name: Decoy
goal: You can lure a king or queen onto a square where a fork, a pin or a mate is waiting.
intro: A decoy lures an enemy piece, usually the king or the queen, onto a bad square. You offer something it has to take, and on its new square a fork, a pin or a mate is waiting. Deflection is about the square a defender leaves; a decoy is about the square a piece lands on.

parts.title: Where should the king stand?
parts.keyIdea: A capture can drag the king onto the square where your knight's fork is waiting.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's rook has just come to g7 to block your rook. Look at the squares your knight can reach, and think about where you would like Black's king to stand.

notes.text: 42.Rxg7 trades the rooks. Black has to take back with the king, because any other move allows mate in one, so the king has to come to g7.
43.Ne8+: the knight checks the king on g7 and attacks the bishop on d6 at the same time. The king must move, and the bishop is lost.
44.Nxd6 takes the bishop. The rook trade brought the king to g7, right where the knight could fork it with the bishop.

parts.title: Where should the queen stand?
parts.keyIdea: Offer a piece the queen has to take, so that it lands on a square your knight can fork.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Your knight on h6 could check the king from f7. Which square would you like Black's queen to be on when it does?

notes.text: 32.Rd8: the rook offers itself on d8 and attacks the queen. The queen is pinned to the king along the back rank, the row the king started on, so it cannot leave that row, and it has little choice but to take the rook.
33.Nf7+: the knight checks from f7 and attacks the queen on d8 at the same time, a fork of king and queen.
34.Nxd8 takes the queen. You gave a rook and won a queen, because the queen was lured onto d8.

parts.title: The long diagonal to h8
parts.keyIdea: A sacrifice with check can drag the king onto a square where its own pieces box it in.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black has just taken your bishop on d5. Your queen's diagonal from c3 runs all the way to h8: where would Black's king have to stand for a queen move there to be mate?

notes.text: 26.Rf8+: the rook offers itself with check. The king has only one move: it must take the rook, because g7 and h8 are covered by your queen and f7 by your pawn on e6. Then the king stands on f8.
27.Qh8#: the queen comes to h8 along the long diagonal and gives check. Black's own bishop on e8 and pawn on e7 block the king, your pawn on e6 covers f7, and the queen covers g7 and g8: mate.

parts.title: King, queen and rook in a row
parts.keyIdea: A trade can pull the queen to a square where your next move pins it to its king with a guarded piece.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White, with two rooks against a queen and a rook. Black's rook has just come to f6 to attack your rook on g6. Black's king, queen and rook all stand on the sixth rank, side by side.

notes.text: 43.Rxf6 trades rooks on f6. If Black does not take back, the rook on f6 pins the queen to the king and takes it next, so the queen takes on f6. There it stands next to g6, where a rook guarded by your h5 pawn can pin it to the king on d6.

44.Rg6: your other rook comes to g6 and pins the queen. Your rook, Black's queen and Black's king now stand on one line, so the queen cannot step off the sixth rank. Whatever Black does, the queen is lost, and the most Black can get for it is your rook.

Black's queen took your rook, and 45.hxg6 takes back. Only kings and pawns are left, and the Engine sees this pawn endgame as a win for you: you are a pawn up and your pawn on g6 is far advanced. It still needs care: Black's king can reach that pawn quickly, so a careless push of it, such as g7 after ...Ke6, lets Black draw.
